en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Verses for the Illumination of the Homage in the *Jinālaṅkāra* (The Ornament of the Conquerors).

He who, for the sake of the world, became a Buddha by renouncing wealth, sons, wife, limbs, and life; having fulfilled the incomparable factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma) belonging to the Thirty-three gods, he attained pure enlightenment that bestows all virtues;
having become the supreme being in the three worlds, he brought an end to suffering and liberated those worthy of vessels from their misery.
Having bowed to the Conqueror, who has accumulated sublime merit and is the sole kinsman of the entire world—
to whom no one is equal and who is supreme in the greatness of his wholesome deeds upon this earth— I shall speak of his vast, stainless, and unsurpassed store of requisites for enlightenment;
listen as I describe the cause that accords with its result, leading to the state of a Sugata.
Verses Illuminating the Perfection of the Yoga Practitioner:

He who was born in the ninth moment as a bearer of the heard Dhamma, with faculties purified by virtue, seeing that saṃsāra is not the goal and perceiving the auspicious state as security that brings about the destruction of existence—
honoring that Sage who teaches the path leading to its attainment, he should then accomplish that auspicious state through the cultivation of mindfulness of the Buddha and other practices.
The Verses for Purifying the Subject Matter:
Who is the Buddha? What are the qualities of a Buddha?
He is he who has attained the state of being beyond thought.
What purpose, not shared with others,
did he accomplish, and what did the Buddha say?
It is established as a certainty that the Buddha is one whose continuum of aggregates is purified.
But it is established as a rule that purity of the continuity of the aggregates is a quality.
On five days he performed his duties,
gladdening the army by means of the power of his supernormal knowledge.
Having understood that the conduct of Janavasabha was conducive [to the Dhamma],
he spoke of the abandonment of underlying tendencies;
this is a verse illustrating what is not shared by others.
He whose infinite virtues have risen high,
like the sole sun in the three realms of the Buddha-field—
he knows this world and the world beyond.
It is both sentient and insentient;
belonging to one's own continuum and that of others,
past, future, and present.
And among the infinite beings in the world-systems,
not even all of them together are equal to him alone;
in the directions such as the east, there are world-spheres—
Even numbering in the thousands, they are immeasurable;
those gods, humans, and Brahmas who have gathered together in one place and are deliberating.
To those possessing name-and-form that has come down from beginningless time,
proceeding according to their respective nature as cause and fruit,
and failing to achieve the state of being or non-being of those [causes],...
They have entered into various types of perversion.
[They do not understand] the occurrence of kamma and the occurrence of its fruit,
nor the nature of phenomena as being characterized by unity, diversity, and lack of effort.
Because it is concealed by the dense continuity of volitional formations,
we are not able to speak of the auspicious and stainless [Nirvana];
that one alone is the maker of peace and the dispeller of darkness.
Having fully understood all that is to be known without exception,
he alone is capable of illuminating the supreme, most wonderful, auspicious, and straight path in their midst.
Thus Gotama, the son of the Sakyas, the Lord of Sages,
who has become a lamp for the entire world,
[liberates] infinite beings from the bondage of existence.
You released [the elephant],
maintaining equanimity toward the fruit of your compassion.
Speak now of his no small merit here, as illustrated by this verse of aspiration.
There exists nothing else superior that is equal to it;
what virtue was given by one who is its peer,
or was it perhaps self-made, or obtained by chance?
Not obtained from another, nor by former Buddhas,
nor through the conventional designation of many such as Brahmā and others,
but by that which is self-made and incomparable—
This is the fruition obtained through giving and other virtues.
From this point, at the end of four hundred thousand and more than a hundred thousand incalculable eons;
At that time, when the past had passed away, the ascetic Sumedha traveled through the air by means of his psychic power.
Then the Conqueror named Dīpaṅkara, together with his Saṅgha, [appeared].
Radiant, he proceeds to the delightful city,
being honored by humans and gods,
like the thousand-rayed sun in the sky.
Having heard that he is the Buddha, he was joyful and delighted, thinking of how he had performed many meritorious deeds;
"Today, by giving this body of mine to him," he thought.
"I shall become a Buddha in a future time.
Having built a bridge over that mud in the depths of the mountain cave,
he lay down there with his very body.
"May this Buddha go upon my back;
if he becomes a Buddha for me in the future,
the Victor shall indeed walk upon the crown of my head."
His aspiration will be fulfilled in the future;
having known this, the Buddha declared it without remainder:
"He shall become a Buddha among those yet to come."
Having heard this, as if he had received a great consecration,
or were recollecting the attainment of enlightenment;
and having paid homage, when the Sage, the God among men, had departed,
Having risen, he reflected upon the ten perfections;
having firmly grasped the thirty perfections and the three trainings in the presence of the Victor.
Though capable of reaching the further shore of existence, he entered existence out of the power of compassion for sentient beings.

Having worshipped each and every one of those incomparable, supreme Victors without exception, this one will certainly become a Buddha; for it was predicted by those various Victors that he would inevitably become a Buddha after worshipping with his head that peerless water-offering.
Enduring each and every suffering, he fulfilled the perfections that bestow all virtues.
This is the verse illustrating the equipment for enlightenment: "He was worn out by the sight of people worn out by suffering..."
He constantly showed compassion toward the people;
for, knowing that this was the means to liberate them,
he took even their offenses upon himself.
Even when given by wicked people, because he has plunged into the oceans of the supreme perfections such as giving and the rest,
no suffering whatsoever, however exceedingly great it may be, [can affect him].
Seeking only the welfare of beings, he did not know [any other purpose].
Having cut off his own head, he gave it away;
having cooked his own flesh, he gave it away.
Thus, when his limbs have already been cut off at the time of his resolve,
what further harm can be done by cutting the one who is already corrupt?
In this way, even though suffering has been experienced throughout hundreds of endless births, [it remains the same].
Having attained [this state], seeking only the welfare of beings,
he protected Dīpaṅkara— who had mastered virtue, concentration, and wisdom—
until he himself reached the foot of the Bodhi tree, having fully perfected his goal.
When the wise one made his resolution,
and when Sivindi gave Maddi— between these two events,
not even a single birth had passed.
It was to no purpose that he came to us;
even compared to a single drop of water in the great ocean,
the number of births within his intestines is not small.
For those who have continuously fulfilled the perfections,
what measure or comparison could there be, or where? [It is like] one who,
on the side of a road, [plants] a sweet mango seed...
For the sake of shade and fruit for the great multitude,
he indeed planted that very moment; by that act,
he obtained the merit of both shade and fruit in the highest realm.
Just so, at the very moment he dedicated himself for the welfare of people on the path of saṃsāra,
merit was already accomplished for him in that regard.
Those who carry away even his life-breath—
he gave blood as deep as the ocean,
and he gave the gift of his own flesh equal to the invincible earth.
He gave [the Bodhisatta] a head with hair reaching down to the ears,
exceeding even Mount Meru in height, and eyes that surpassed the stars in the sky.
— Verses illustrating the descent into the womb.
For, crossing with steadfastness over the oceans of giving profound drinks and so forth,
and having brought the perfections (pāramī) to completion through the gift of his own flesh,
he dwelt in the Tusita body until the ripening of enlightenment was reached.
And at the entreaty of the gods, he entered the womb of his mother.
Mindful and clearly comprehending, he descended into the mother’s womb;
at the moment of his descent, the entire ten-thousandfold world system trembled.
Then there were thirty-two auspicious omens at that time;
with a heart joyful and elated, the mother beheld her son within her womb.
(Verses illustrating the auspicious signs of childbirth)
When her pregnancy was full, after ten months had passed,
she went to the blossoming and excellent Lumbinī grove;
standing there, she grasped a branch of a noble sāla tree.
She gave birth to that excellent son in comfort.
At that time, throughout the ten thousandfold world-systems,
the devas, nāgas, asuras, and yakkhas—
From various directions,
auspiciousness came to the auspicious Cakkavāḷa;
manifold-branched and with a thousand circles, it arrived.
The gods held up a parasol in the sky;
golden-handled yak-tail whisks fell down,
drums were beaten, and conchs resounded.
Unstained even by mud,
standing still with his feet outstretched,
like a preacher entering the Dharma-seat.
Just as the supreme sun rises from the sky,
the ones whose taints were exhausted approached and received him with a golden net, having entered the assembly of Brahmās.
Then the gods [received it] with an antelope skin,
and then humans [received] it with fine linen;
from their hands, he stood upon the excellent ground.
He surveyed all directions on every side;
and the gods of the Brahma-realm proclaimed:
"Nowhere is there anyone equal to you, nor any superior."
Having taken seven strides to the north,
he let out a lion’s roar to make it heard by those deities.
Then, taking her son, the mother went to her own dwelling.
The mother went on the seventh day and attained the state of being the giver of sons.
Those two, who possessed excellent marks, were well-fed by the Brahmin on the fifth day,
so that he might take their names.
Having seen this, they raised a single finger, thinking:
"This one will become a Buddha, free from passion.
And having seen one who was old, one who was sick, and one who was dead...
Seeing one who has been summoned and one who has gone forth,
he abandons the going-forth and pursues sensual pleasures;
this one will become a Buddha, free from passion.
A Stanza Illustrating the Attainments of a Householder:
Like the moon increasing in its course, he caused his family to prosper;
like the sun in the sky, he bestowed gifts through the arising of his merit.
For Siddhattha, having obtained Queen Yasodharā,
was preceded by forty thousand women; he dwelt in houses that were delightful,
most delightful, and beautiful.
In accordance with the three seasons,
he enjoyed that happiness as if it were divine bliss—
the wondrous and marvelous royal splendor.
A Single Stanza Illuminating the Inclination Toward Renunciation:
Homage to him, the one of great majesty, for whom darkness does not exist;
who, having seen the signs that shatter pride, [is free from it].
Laziness is a deformity that cuts away joy;
evil deeds cut away happiness;
but the wisdom gained cuts away existence.
Like a house on fire, the Great Seer went forth, abandoning his terrifying cry; having beheld the Great Seer,
his own son, who was like a god.
You create for yourself a great flood of passion,
having pulled yourself up step by step from the threshold of the threshold of the hellish donkey of torment.
Enough, enough with further ornamentation; let the mind go like a mind toward the destruction of the bodiless one (the god of love).
The great seer has reached the threshold of the threshold.
He reflected upon the destruction of the limbs of passion:
"What use is this to me, who stand at the mouth of old age and death,
and who am no longer under my own control but subject to the power of sensual desire?"
Liberation is not to be accomplished by desire through desire,
nor is there anything for me to be gained by pride through pride;
for Māra, together with his host, is indeed irresistible.
As if crushing sugarcane with a machine, you crush me.
To those people who are burning, scorched by heat, and exhausted— without protection, shelter, or refuge— you [are their protector].
Having seen it again and again, how could I,
by means of desire, dispel that which is auspicious for you?
For this very one who has passed away from ignorance through true knowledge— how could I lead him astray?
People have fallen into a state where the essence is perceived as non-essence;
I, being joined with true knowledge and having fallen away from ignorance,
am able to deliver them, though I have gone beyond all attachment.
"Is this path not the liberation from the thicket of views?"—
thus did the people unanimously say, "It is the highest!
Alas, it is naked, a mere faction within the darkness of delusion!
I shall destroy that host, the foremost of paths.
People produce only further birth for those who see suffering as something not to be endured through the manner of one who observes.
Those who see only the suffering that must be endured do not understand the source from which evil arises. They are bound by the floods,
the yokes, the taints, and the defilements.
Those very things that have arisen from it destroy it:
birth, aging, and death are absolute,
and misfortune is constant and manifold.
Seeing that the latent tendencies of beings have long been burning with defilements, the Self-Existent One said:
"I shall realize enlightenment and discipline sentient beings."
Even later, I saw that Suttanta which was heard:
"That divine wheel, with its rim of sharp blades—
a kingdom full of passion, intoxication, and revelry."
Those other kinsmen have come to bondage;
this son, born of a slave-girl, is the messenger of the bodiless god of love.
Yet, he dwells in the radiant glory of his virtue.
This is a fortress of venomous snakes,
filled with great poison; these young women,
though radiant, are like thorny brambles when one touches them.
She whose splendor is radiant, yet for whom even such splendor does not exist—
having beheld her, there is no satiety for those possessed by desire.
Come now, let me go to that forest grove where her head is severed.
Moving with the playful gait of a lion upon the frontal globes of intoxicated elephants—
O Ananga, whose arrows have long since been spent,
withdraw your shafts; cease from this pursuit!
One who has reached the end of suffering through restraint does not grieve for the mind;
seeing that grief is not found here, I go toward peace.
Delight is found in the five strands of sensual pleasure, but delight is found in seclusion.
Thinking only of what was sufficient for himself,
he departed from there and there like a fool who has seen the abode of the mind, the abode of the source of the mind's desires.
Verses Illuminating the Wonder of the Lifting of the Footstool:
As long as the sun continues to move, obstructed by Mount Meru,
and as long as the Wheel-Treasure proceeds in the world;
How could that Lord of the Island, who traverses the sky, has conquered the four quarters,
and is free from desire, ever abandon his course?
On this island of more than two thousand four hundred leagues, he is the great one.
Even there, having abandoned the most excellent and beloved,
noble Jambudīpa— the delightful city of Kapilavatthu, which was like the very navel of the earth—
how indeed could he, free from all longing, lift up his foot?
From the clan of eighty kinsmen, there were indeed a thousand Śākyas,
owners of elephants, grain, and wealth, who had conquered hosts of enemies;
from among them, by lineage, he became a Gotama, the foremost delighter of his father.
Having abandoned that delightful dwelling, so enchanting to inhabit and radiant with jewels—
even in summer it was wondrous and like a celestial palace—
how indeed could he, free from desire, lift his foot?
How could he, having abandoned his white parasol and the fluttering banners and flags raised aloft, have taken that step free from desire?
There were four lotus ponds with their lotuses.
The blossoms were scattered all around the temple;
the cuckoos cried out above in their sweet warbling.
How could he, having abandoned hope, have lifted his foot to depart?
Upon every lotus, rows of bees were crying out;
from all sides she quickly saw the cage.
Having seen the lotuses, [she looked] at her own lotus-face.
They shrink back as if out of shame before the Lord.
Sweet and warbling sweetly,
the swarms of bees move from lotus to lotus.
Why has the bee now made its dwelling in honey that has been abandoned by its master?
Having taken the essence from there, the bees have carried it to their own home.
Resounding with a sweet, harmonious melody,
they surpass all other sounds with their song as they play the lute;
thus do those women dance, as if in the city of the gods.
Urged on, with full breasts and lips,
radiant with the girdle of the bodiless god (Kāma),
she was always a giver of delightful contact, like a celestial maiden.
The women, adorned with excellent armlets and anklets,
delight in their play; their passion inflamed by passion,
they strike cymbals on every side.
Rising to many thousands of cubits in height,
they challenged him, saying, "Is even Sakka equal to a Śākya?
They were large-eyed, smiling, and possessed of beautiful waists.
The women of Nimbattana, their voices raised in songs of wonder,
adorned with ornaments, wearing garlands, and well-dressed,
danced while being cheered by those beating the rhythmic instruments.
For those for whom there is no comparison in the world,
there is indeed no room for talk regarding their tactile sensations;
experiencing such delight in sensual pleasures, [they do not know the bliss of renunciation].
Having abandoned hope, how indeed could he lift his foot?
At every step, she sang and sang again, her bracelets, tinkling girdle,
and lute sounding in harmony, as she sang song after song that brought delight to her husband.
In hand after hand, bracelets jingle with a flurry as they rush about in agitation;
seeing them again and again, one wonders, "Alas, alas! What is this pursuit that brings such delight?
This is a verse illuminating the departure from which there is no returning.
By that merit accumulated over an infinite time, which produced for him a celestial mansion as a vehicle,
on that very day his wife gave birth to a son.
Having abandoned them, that Sugata has gone as one who has truly gone.
Having left behind his father and mother while they were still living,
as well as those kinsmen and such women;
Having abandoned such delightful dwellings,
that Sugata has gone as one who has truly gone.
[He left behind] linen, fine wool, silk, and Chinese cloth.
Clad in garments from Sāketa, fragrant with excellent perfumes,
he shone like Vāsava;
having abandoned [the world], he has gone like the Sugata who has gone.
The four treasures, clearly manifested,
have arisen as the upholders of beings, the earth that sustains all;
they are the ground for the dwelling of beings, the source of the essence of purity.
Having abandoned it, that Sugata has gone, like one who has truly gone.
In a beautiful golden bowl adorned with a hundred royal lines,
there was excellent, fragrant, and pure rice-food.
Having lived among his own people and the courtesans,
that Sugata departed, having abandoned them like one who has gone [to the forest].
With his own fragrant scent, he was not made empty by the pleasant scents [of others].
With his body anointed with fragrant scents and his limbs well-fanned by fragrant breezes, that Sugata has departed,
having left behind [this world] like one who has already gone.
With limbs distinguished by excellent marks,
adorned with celestial ornaments,
he shines brilliantly with his peerless royal garments.
Having abandoned them, that Sugata has gone as one who has truly gone.
He left behind various seats, couches, and dwellings—
resplendent and shining like mines of jewels.
There, those [trees] were adorned with jeweled banners;
having abandoned them, they became like drops of frost.
Blazing with various kinds of radiant jewels,
I am constantly praised by women and by mansions adorned with royal parasols, the wheel-treasure, and other ornaments;
thus I move here and there, honored by the voices of men.
A Two-Lined Yamaka Verse:
[I salute] Yaśodharā, whose lips were full-breasted,
and whose limbs served as the banners for the theater of the bodiless god of love.
Having abandoned that which is brightened by celestial nymphs and full of obstacles,
he has surely gone like the Sugata;
he radiates a mind of natural dispassion and splendor.
The mendicant has gathered his alms and finished his meal;
having abandoned even that beautiful and excellent Yasodharā,
he has surely departed like the Sugata.
Pure and pure he wandered about, sword in hand;
better than having women was being free from the scent of women;
though he abandoned glory, he did not abandon his woman.
Having abandoned these dull things, the Tathāgata has gone forth.
Though his skin was green by the power of passion for the queen,
he did not recall the embrace through the mark of the avatthā-plant.
He who once indulged in sensual pleasure has now abandoned that very pleasure;
he has surely departed like the Sugata,
dwelling in solitude throughout immeasurable eons.
Having abandoned the glory of sovereignty and his beloved wife,
he praised that ancient [renunciation] as a tailor points out a tiny flaw in a garment.
Thinking "So be it," he now raised up Yaśodharā like a banner;
intoxicated with the thought "I have conquered," the kinsman of the negligent—
He saw no interval between the arising of knowledge and its seat.
Having seen existence as the source of the fire of suffering,
he brought about the breaking up of the factors that produce it.
Having abandoned Yaśodharā, whose breasts and lips were full,
he went to the state that is the domain of the Buddha’s power;
for infinite beings throughout infinite time.
The Bodiless One has conquered those whose cause is the bodiless [mind];
indeed, he alone has been defeated,
for that Tathāgata does not return again.
Having seen the interval between the falling away of knowledge,
that Tathāgata does not return;
that Tathāgata does not return.
Having seen the falling of the seat of knowledge,
there then occurred for him a verse of triple-footed yamaka, a marvel of the Tathāgata.
For thus Māra spoke of peace when it was falsely attributed to burning;
for thus even Māra then spoke of that peace,
for thus even Māra then laughed at her.
The Great Yamaka Verse on the Footstep: He who has conquered his desires and is disciplined, he who has conquered his desires and is disciplined;
he who has reached the end and is self-controlled, he who has reached the end and is self-controlled.
The giver of his own desire, the one who has trained in the discipline and is infinite in virtue;
the giver of his own desire, the one who has trained in the discipline and is infinite in virtue. This is the verse on the interlocking yamaka figures without repetition at the beginning or end.
O you who are terrifying with your fierce pride and ferocity, O you who roar like a thundering cloud, O you who roar with a sound as formidable as a crashing storm!
O you who have destroyed all arrogance through your roar!
The Victor, the Sun, caused the world to rejoice with his roar;
in this verse of reverse *yamaka*,
time, by its very nature as the world’s course, did not fail to attend to distinction.
Time has not passed without my cultivating excellence through the state of the world;
by me was composed this *Viśeṣa*, endowed with the glory of the King of Kings,
which is cherished for its long-cultivated essence and which destroys the decay of age.
The Yamaka-gāthā beginning with *Ekaṭhānika*:
O you who grasp the river of doubt, O you who desire the limbs of desire, O you who speak of desire! Where, where is doubt for one who grasps the river of doubt? Hā hā! Where is doubt? Where is it?
Free from immodesty, free from immodesty; without delusion, do not be deluded.
He spoke of liberation as the entrance to the path, O Great One, which is capable of dispelling the confusion of delusion.
Seeing the non-arising of evil, he has risen above the non-arising of evil.
Free from attachment to evil and the states of existence arising from evil, having reached the state beyond evil and existence;
seeing both the wholesome and the unwholesome, he abandoned both the wholesome and the unwholesome;
detached from the wholesome and the unwholesome, he passed away from the wholesome and the unwholesome.
A Yāmaka-gāthā with Excess Syllables:
Nonānino nanūnāni nanenāni nanānino,
Nunnānenāni nūna na nānanaṃ nānanena no.
In the midst of gods and asuras, he is the essence, the one whose voice flows with the essence of the nectar;
in the nectar that is the essence of flavors, he flowed within the splendor of gods and asuras.
He is the god who delights the gods, yet, O God of Gods, there is no delight for us.
The Knower of the Vedas, the Veda, and the knowledge of the Vedas,
that God of Gods sat upon his divine throne in the Sasāsana monastery and taught the Seat of Vision to the gods who were seated there.
The riddle verse:
The one who has transcended the ten taints is conscious; like the sun, he is the dispeller of darkness for the blind.
With his intention as full as the eighth day of the lunar fortnight, he has appeared as if he were not otherwise.
The Verse on the Pervasive Twin-Miracles:
The Great Sage was solely intent upon the welfare of others,
solely through the power of the ten perfections.
By that power of the Māra-force, he was utterly defeated;
yet by that very same power, he attained the most perfectly pure enlightenment.
—Verses Illuminating the Great Struggle (Mahāpadhānadīpanīgāthā)
Having gone with his well-concealed, well-harnessed horse, he whose evil nature was cast off, that peerless being,
reached the shore of the peerless [ocean].
Having gone forth as one peerless,
he obtained in the Anūpiya mango grove a spiritual joy and happiness that was incomparable.
He made the city of Rājagaha, including the king and his retinue, appear beautiful despite its ugliness; then,
[he went] to the ascetics of Aḷāra and Udaka.
Leaving behind the abode with a mind satisfied by jhāna,
he went to the land of Uruvelā for the Great Striving and performed difficult austerities until he reached the pinnacle.
All-knowledge is not accomplished through desire, nor is it accomplished through what is excessively difficult; it is accomplished through the middle way.
Having understood that, one should cultivate the previously acquired qualities.
He went forth to bring together the Dhamma of perfect enlightenment.
In the field of the Buddhas of the three times, he is the triple white umbrella; this is the verse illustrating the defeat of Māra.
Having attained this, he shall become a lord of the world;
having gone to the invincible seat of enlightenment,
he sat immovable for battle with Māra.
Having given me his flesh and his kingdom at that time,
my father Suddhodana paid homage with his head and worshipped me with a white parasol.
He himself possessed the strength of Nārāyaṇa and had reached the further shore of the power of higher knowledge (abhiññā).
To conquer the entire world, he approached the seat of enlightenment.
At that time, King Vasavatti, the lord of the six realms of sense-desire,
accompanied by his army and vehicles, approached the seat of enlightenment for battle.
"Come, bind him, tie him up, and guard this servant!
Born from human filth, does he not realize what he is doing here?
He causes a vast, ninefold rain to fall, burning down everything."
Having created a cloud of smoke, he hurled many swords;
yet even while hurling discus-weapons, he was unable to achieve anything, for seeing no way to seize his prey, he spoke thus:
"There is nothing to be grasped."
"Siddhattha, why have you come to sit upon my seat?
Arise from this seat, or else I shall break your heart!
Seeing your young son playing at my feet—"
The father looked upon Māra with loving-kindness and compassion;
then the Sage uttered an unassailable lion’s roar:
"This wretch does not know that I am dear to him even in the state of a slave."
Born by whatever karma into a superior city of the gods,
not knowing his own destiny, he imagines himself to be the Eldest of the World.
For whatever merit has been performed by beings in the pit of the infinite world, [it is thus].
It does not equal even a sixteenth part of my own single perfection.
Having become a hare among the animals, upon seeing a supplicant who had come,
I cooked my own flesh and gave it to him on the glowing embers.
Who else, being of sound mind and conscious, would perform such difficult austerities throughout endless ages?
Yet this very body has been perfected through such infinite merits.
Not knowing things as they truly are, one imagines, "I am a human being.
I am neither a human nor a non-human, neither Brahmā nor a deity;
I have come here only to show aging and death to the world.
"Unstained by the world, I am born as a Conqueror of the infinite;
having become a Buddha at the foot of the Bodhi tree, I shall deliver the vast multitude of people.
Having seen Māra, who bears his banner on all sides, together with his mount, in battle—"
I go forth to battle; do not displace me from my station.
That army which neither the world nor the devas can withstand, I shall crush with my wisdom, like an unripe vessel with a stone.
Desiring [to see him], I paced back and forth within a pod the size of a mustard seed;
desiring [to see him], I covered the world-system with my own body.
Having seized all these, I could crush them in a mere finger-snap.
I possess strength and power, yet the taking of life is not permitted for me.
Of what use is the weapon or the might of this gadfly?
For it is not even fitting for me to converse with such a being on account of that evil.
"What need have I for another witness for my resolve?
This great earth, shaken by the gift of Maddi, shall be my witness.
Having said this, he prostrated his right arm upon the ground.
Then the earth trembled and a great roar arose.
With the roar of the earth, thunder crashed and lightning flashed in the sky;
Māra, together with his retinue, stood in its midst, terrified by fear.
Like ashes stirred up by a great wind, you were scattered;
a great roar arose: "Victory for Siddhattha!

In this present life and in all previous existences,
